ABSTRACT Severe data starvation, architectural heterogeneity and Byzantine vulnerabilities fundamentally impede the deployment of robust multiclass classification models in decentralised edge environments. To address these intertwined challenges, we propose fusion isomerism learning (FusionIL) , a secure and domain‐agnostic framework that synergistically orchestrates isomerism large language models (IsoLLMs), consortium blockchain technology and heterogeneous federated learning. Unlike conventional approaches, FusionIL leverages a trusted committee of permissioned nodes to generate high‐fidelity synthetic data via feature‐driven textual prompts, forming IsoLLMs that capture structural heterogeneity across models. To prevent malicious data pollution, these generated samples undergo rigorous quantitative validation and are securely anchored via the practical Byzantine fault tolerance (PBFT) consensus mechanism. Furthermore, to mitigate the risk of generative model collapse, permissionless edge clients construct “synthetic interleaved datasets” by merging these verified synthetic samples with their private data under strict minority proportions. Subsequently, the framework employs the decentralised heterogeneous integration algorithm (DHIA) to mathematically reconcile and aggregate gradient updates from structurally diverse local models. This architectural innovation effectively eliminates the rigid homogeneity constraints of traditional federated networks. Extensive empirical evaluations across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the synthetic interleaving strategy significantly enhances data diversity and global convergence. Consequently, FusionIL achieves competitive or leading performance against state‐of‐the‐art centralized and federated baselines in classification accuracy and system resilience, establishing a robust paradigm for secure, heterogeneous collaborative learning.

This special issue explores the profound intersection of machine learning, language, and pedagogy, questioning the fundamental role of artificial intelligence in educational and linguistic coordination. Rooted in the age-old dream of combinatorial devices – echoing historical figures from Ramon Llull to Jorge Luis Borges – the collection investigates whether language and thought can be automated without appeals to meaning and reference. As generative AI becomes ubiquitous, we confront a landscape where machines train humans, write academic prose, and simulate understanding. This issue brings together philosophers of technology, linguists, and educational theorists to analyze this paradigm shift. It spans historical genealogies of educational automation, the cognitive potential of human-AI interfaces, and empirical studies on AI literacy and coaching, alongside critical examinations of AI detection systems and the capacity of machines to truly “think”. Furthermore, a dedicated subsection reflects on Borges’s 1937 essay “Ramon Llull’s Thinking Machine,” using this historical lens to dissect contemporary generative models. Taken together, the collected papers reveal an increasingly recursive relationship between machine learning and human learning, bringing questions of epistemic agency, disciplinary expertise, semantic judgement, and evaluative competence to the center of debates about what it means to learn in an age of generative AI. This issue frames these diverse contributions, charting a course through the promises and perils of the automated word.

ABSTRACT Rapid advancement of wearable electronics, the Internet of Things, and artificial intelligence has generated a growing demand for flexible sensors capable of reliable and high‐precision pressure monitoring under complex conditions. However, traditional piezoresistive sensors often suffer from sensitivity degradation and structural fatigue caused by moisture exposure and long‐term cyclic loading. Here, we report a ternary composite aerogel‐based piezoresistive sensor composed of tobacco stem‐derived TEMPO‐oxidized cellulose nanofibers (TTOCNFs), MXene, and polymethylsilsesquioxane (PMSQ) through cross‐scale interfacial engineering. In this design, TTOCNFs form a flexible skeleton, MXene establishes an efficient conductive network, and PMSQ reinforces the framework while imparting hydrophobicity, mitigating moisture‐induced performance degradation. An ice‐templating strategy further constructs a honeycomb‐like skeleton, enabling efficient stress distribution under mechanical deformation. Benefiting from these structural and interfacial synergies at different scales, the sensor exhibits high sensitivity (1612.8 kPa −1 ), broad detection range (2.4 Pa–48.8 kPa), rapid response and recovery (117 and 80 ms), and outstanding cycling stability (>1000 cycles), while maintaining reliable performance in humid environments. It enables high‐fidelity monitoring of subtle physiological signals and human motions, demonstrating strong potential for health monitoring and human‐machine interaction. This work provides a scalable and sustainable design strategy for environmentally robust aerogel‐based pressure sensors toward smart wearable electronics.

The article provides a theoretical generalization and develops a practical mechanism for the anti-crisis financial management of an insurance company amidst the growing intensity of cyberattacks and resulting digital shocks. The study analyzes the contemporary operating environment of the Ukrainian insurance market, characterized by high military-economic uncertainty, strict regulatory oversight by the National Bank of Ukraine on compliance with capital and solvency requirements, and accelerated digitalization of business processes. The widespread adoption of online sales and automated claims settlement, alongside business advantages, has created high technological dependence and qualitatively new threats to insurers’ financial stability. The study aims to substantiate the conceptual foundations and develop a comprehensive anti-crisis mechanism for an insurance company’s financial management to ensure its liquidity, solvency, and operational continuity under conditions of digital shocks. In the research process, a set of scientific methods was applied: systemic, structural-functional, and comparative analysis – to examine the impact factors of the digital environment and assess the limitations of traditional anti-crisis management approaches; statistical, economic-mathematical, and graphical analysis—to study the dynamics, structure, and vectors of cyberattacks on the financial sector of Ukraine in 2025; and scientific modeling—to develop the multi-level architecture of the anti-crisis mechanism. The results confirm that the financial sector remains a primary target for cybercriminals, with malware distribution, phishing, and account compromise as the main tools. It was established that classic anti-crisis management instruments, focused on retrospective ratio analysis, static reserves, and standard budgeting, prove ineffective against the high velocity of digital shock propagation, which can trigger immediate cash gaps, premium inflow disruption, and reputational damage. The research’s scientific novelty lies in developing an author-designed adaptive mechanism for anti-crisis financial management, enabling a qualitative shift from passive loss coverage to proactively building an insurer’s digital resilience. The novelty comprises measures structured across three temporal and functional levels: the preventive level involves establishing an early warning system for digital crises and modeling combined cyber scenarios within solvency stress testing; the operational level encompasses forming a targeted reserve for financial adaptation and cyber resilience along with dynamic management of highly liquid assets; the strategic level is based on cyber risk transfer through reinsurance, IT security cost optimization, and the full integration of cyber risk management into corporate governance. The practical significance of the results is that executive management in insurance companies can directly implement the proposed tools and algorithms to rapidly neutralize digital threats, maintain payment channel continuity, and preserve high customer trust during crises. Future research could develop mathematical models to formalize early-warning indicators of a digital crisis using Artificial Intelligence and Big Data, and refine actuarial calculations to determine the optimal volume of the financial adaptation reserve. Keywords: digitalization, insurance services, anti-crisis management.

The article examines the aspects of the digital transformation of industrial enterprises amid technological, economic, and institutional change. The study is relevant because digital transformation has moved beyond implementing individual information systems and technological solutions to encompass changes in business processes, organizational approaches, management systems, resource utilization, and mechanisms for creating economic value. For Ukrainian industrial enterprises, this issue has become particularly urgent because they must simultaneously restore production capacity, modernize technology, maintain operational resilience, and adapt to the new requirements of the digital economy. The study aims to analyze and systematize the theoretical and methodological framework for developing mechanisms for industrial enterprises’ digital transformation. To achieve this purpose, the article clarifies the concepts of “digitization,” “digitalization,” and “digital transformation.” It establishes that the digital transformation of an industrial enterprise should be viewed as a systemic process of restructuring technological, production, managerial, organizational, and market relationships through the integration of digital technologies, data, and digital competencies. Unlike fragmented automation of individual operations, digital transformation involves extending technological changes across interconnected business processes, the management system, and value-creation mechanisms. The conditions for digital transformation in industrial enterprises fall into four main groups: technological, organizational, resource-related, and institutional. Technological conditions include digital infrastructure, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, robotics, big data, and digital twins; organizational and intangible conditions include digital culture, competencies, organizational flexibility, strategic orientation, managerial support, and data governance; resource-related conditions include financial, investment, human, information, and time resources; institutional conditions include public policy, financial support, the regulatory environment, the innovation ecosystem, and international integration. This study examines current trends in digital development in enterprises in the European Union and Ukraine and identifies differences in the adoption of basic and advanced digital technologies. For Ukrainian industrial enterprises, insufficient financial and human capacity to scale digital solutions remains a significant constraint, particularly amid wartime uncertainty and competition for resources between restoring production capacities and investing in digital solutions. The mechanism for ensuring digital transformation should be an integrated system of interconnected technological, organizational, financial, human-resource, informational, and institutional components. Align the digital strategy with the enterprise’s overall development strategy, secure adequate resources and financial support, develop employees’ digital competencies, integrate digital technologies into key business processes, and account for digital maturity, financial capacity, production-specific characteristics, and external environmental risks. Keywords: digital transformation, digitalization, industrial enterprises, financial support, digital investments, financial mechanisms, digital maturity.

The article substantiates a methodology for developing the Russian communicative competence of Uzbek-speaking students using generative artificial intelligence. The study is relevant due to the contradiction between the high linguodidactic potential of large language models and the lack of methodological solutions addressing Uzbek and Russian typological differences and cross-linguistic interference. The theoretical framework integrates competence-based, communicative and contrastive approaches, the technological pedagogical content knowledge model and formative assessment. Russian and international research on generative artificial intelligence in language teaching is analysed, revealing a shortage of studies on Turkic-speaking learners and criterion-referenced assessment. The methodology is implemented through a four-stage cycle comprising diagnostic, generative interactive, reflective corrective and assessment stages, governed by the principles of teacher expert control, transparency and academic integrity. It provides contrastive feedback that explains errors through comparison with the learners’ native language system. Diagnostics, assessment and evaluation are differentiated, and the use of analytic rubrics and performance-based assessment is justified. Experimental teaching shows statistically significant growth in the interactive and pragmatic components of communicative competence and fewer interference errors in the experimental group. The limitations of the methodology, critical verification of machine-generated text as a transferable skill and the changing professional role of the teacher are discussed. The findings apply to teaching Russian at Uzbek universities and teacher development.

The article examines a methodology for enhancing students’ intellectual-communicative competence in inclusive higher education through the pedagogically grounded use of artificial intelligence. Drawing on approaches to communicative competence, competency-based learning, Universal Design for Learning, and AI-assisted language education, intellectual-communicative competence is defined as an integrative ability to analyze information, formulate and justify a position, interact effectively in a foreign language, and regulate learning through reflection. A four-component structure is proposed, comprising motivational-axiological, cognitive-intellectual, communicative-activity, and reflective-regulatory components. The study substantiates a methodological cycle of “diagnosis – intellectualization – communication – feedback – reflection” and identifies conditions for its implementation in an inclusive environment, including personalization, differentiation, accessibility, critical verification of AI-generated responses, and teacher mediation. The article argues that artificial intelligence should function as a cognitive-communicative tool rather than a source of ready-made answers and concludes that the proposed model requires experimental validation in authentic educational settings.

ABSTRACT Human error in emergency departments (EDs) arises from contextual human factors and individual cognitive differences, yet these streams are often studied separately. This study models ED nurse performance and error risk using artificial neural networks (ANNs), with decision‐making styles (DMSs) as a moderating variable. Twenty factors contributing to human error (FCHE) were identified and refined by ED experts. Data from 239 emergency nurses in three Iranian military hospitals over 1 year included incident‐based FCHE scores, a 40‐item performance instrument, and Driver et al.‘s DMS questionnaire. Reliability and validity were confirmed, and aspect weights were derived using the Best–Worst Method. Multilayer perceptron (MLP) and radial basis function networks were trained with leakage‐free fivefold cross‐validation. The MLP achieved an MSE of 0.0584 on a held‐out 15% test set, outperforming regression baselines. Efficiency scores were validated against DEA and sensitivity analysis ranked influential factors by DMS, supporting targeted staffing and decision‐support design.

Purpose: The aim of this study is the investigation of the moderating role of general attitudes towards artificial intelligence in the relationship between medical error attitudes (causes of medical errors and medical error approaches) and proactive behaviour, within the context of social cognitive theory. Methodology: The study was conducted using a quantitative research approach. The study sample included 399 healthcare workers identified using convenience sampling. The research data were collected at two different points in time using a time-lagged data collection method; analyses were carried out after the data obtained from the two data collection processes were matched. Findings: The research found that both the causes of medical errors and medical error approaches have a positive and significant effect on proactive behaviour. Similarly, it was found that general attitudes towards artificial intelligence also have a positive effect on proactive behaviour. However, the results of the moderation analysis indicate that general attitudes towards artificial intelligence act as a moderator in the effect of the causes of medical errors and medical error approaches on proactive behaviour. Accordingly, it was determined that where general attitudes towards artificial intelligence are high, the positive effect of the causes of medical errors and medical error approaches on proactive behaviour is weakened. Originality: This study contributes to extending Social Cognitive Theory in the context of attitudes toward emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence in healthcare. The findings demonstrate that the influence of individual cognitive factors on behaviour differs across contexts and contribute to the literature by explaining the relationship between attitudes toward medical errors, general attitudes toward artificial intelligence, and the proactive behaviour of healthcare professionals.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has become a prevalent tool in higher education, yet little is known about how its use affects the learning experiences of minority‐ethnic international students (MEIS). Drawing on an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and a four‐strand engagement model, this quantitative study surveyed 273 MEIS across UK business schools and analysed the data with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS‐SEM). The findings suggest that performance expectancy, effort expectancy and social influence predicted intention, and facilitating conditions and intention were also positively associated with self‐reported GAI use frequency. GAI frequency positively predicted cognitive, behavioural, emotional and, most strongly, agentic engagement. Multigroup analysis revealed that female students showed stronger effects of effort expectancy, performance expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions on intention than males; low‐experience students were more sensitive to effort expectancy than high‐experience peers; and postgraduate students exhibited stronger facilitating conditions, performance expectancy and social influence effects than undergraduates. The study highlights both theoretical and practical implications by linking GAI adoption with multidimensional student engagement, with the strongest association observed for agentic engagement, and calls for equity‐focused policy, curriculum interventions and institutional support targeted at individual access gaps among MEIS. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic? Generative AI (GAI) technologies are increasingly used by students in higher education for learning support. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) has been widely applied to examine technology adoption in educational contexts. What this paper adds? It extends UTAUT to an under‐researched population (MEIS), who often face heightened academic, technological and cultural challenges in UK higher education. GAI use by MEIS is strongly associated with cognitive, behavioural, emotional and especially agentic engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy Institutions should consider embedding GAI literacy and access support into orientation and academic skills programmes for MEIS. Educators who integrate GAI into teaching may consider structured questioning, verification and reflection activities while evaluating rather than assuming their effects on engagement. Policymakers should develop equity‐oriented strategies that support the digital and cultural integration of disadvantaged student groups.

Driven by the rapid development of artificial intelligence and the internet of things, flexible piezoelectric polymers and smart sensors have emerged as core research focuses on flexible electronics. Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) and its copolymer P(VDF‐TrFE) stand out for outstanding flexibility, easy fabrication, stable chemical properties, and biocompatibility, holding great promise for flexible sensing and mechanical energy harvesting. However, their inferior piezoelectric coefficients restrict large‐scale practical use relative to inorganic piezoelectric counterparts. Nanofiller doping and three‐dimensional structure design are proven to be efficient ways for improvement of their piezoelectric performance. Herein, MXene‐modified P(VDF‐TrFE) nanofiber piezoelectric devices with 3D spring architecture are prepared through electrospinning and shaping methods for synergistic performance enhancement. The optimized composite film obtains a piezoelectric coefficient of −20.1 pC/N, about 62.1% enhancement compared with pristine samples. The 3D spring structure further improves mechanical adaptability and electric output capacity. The assembled vibration energy harvester reaches a power density of 35.4 mW/m 3 under a 20 MΩ load. Moreover, the fabricated device enables vibration frequency detection and real‐time human sleep monitoring, showing vast application potential in industrial sensing and smart health monitoring.

This conceptual working paper develops NEOMANITAI as a research framework for describing human-AI interaction across digital, embodied and collective settings. It revises an existing umbrella proposal and distinguishes programme names, classification facets, concepts, observations and evidential claims. The edition presents eight ordering conventions, seven descriptive facets, a small typed relation model, three constructed civilian cases and four comparative research questions. The proposed contribution is an inspectable connection between programme navigation, episode descriptions and claim-level provenance. Its usefulness remains to be tested against simpler descriptions and existing approaches. The paper builds on selected historical programme documents and a targeted literature review covering distributed cognition, socio-technical systems, hybrid intelligence, collective intelligence, agents, human-robot interaction, conceptual work and taxonomy development. It reports no new participant data, empirical validation, global novelty finding or established disciplinary status. The constructed cases are explanatory examples. The English paper includes a German abstract. The accompanying JSON contains the conceptual model, examples and recorded literature reading scope. Construction health and safety management has traditionally prioritized physical hazards through regulatory compliance, engineering controls and behavioral safety approaches. Limited attention has been paid to how cognitive and sensory diversity interact with hazard recognition, safety communication and decision-making. This study examined practices reported by construction health and safety officers and site managers for supporting neurodivergent workers during routine construction operations. An exploratory qualitative survey was conducted with 13 health and safety officers and eight site managers in Gauteng Province, South Africa. Twenty-one of 38 invited practitioners completed five open-ended questions. Reflexive thematic analysis identified five related findings. Cognitive and sensory demands were recognized informally but rarely incorporated into risk assessments. Multimodal and simplified communication was valued but inconsistently applied. Supervisors received limited formal preparation. Workplace adjustments were mainly informal or proposed rather than embedded within safety systems. Evaluation continued to rely on conventional lagging indicators. These findings identify a system-design gap rather than locating risk within neurodivergent workers. The study contributes a construction-specific pathway linking site conditions, neurocognitive variation, safety processes, response practices and perceived outcomes. As the evidence reflects practitioner perceptions rather than verified diagnoses or measured safety outcomes, causal conclusions are not supported. The study recommends integrating cognitive ergonomics, psychosocial risk management, supervisor development and leading indicators into routine construction safety systems to strengthen hazard recognition, worker wellbeing and organizational learning.

The article econometrically assesses the impact of human capital on the development of Uzbekistan's digital economy under the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, using data for 2010-2024. A three-component composite digital economy index (DEI) is constructed, and human capital is proxied by tertiary enrolment. Autoregressive distributed lag (ADL) models are estimated with Newey-West (HAC) standard errors, including a regime dummy and an interaction term for the AI policy period. The long-run effect of human capital on the DEI is 0.460; its effect on ICT service exports was statistically insignificant before 2021, while in the AI policy period the short-run elasticity reached 1.04 and the long-run elasticity 1.46. Policy proposals for enriching human capital with AI competencies are developed.

Purpose This conceptual study examines how an AI-enabled Project Management Office (A-PMO) can be understood as a second-order observing system rather than merely as an instrument that observes and controls projects. Drawing primarily on Heinz von Foerster and positioning his work in relation to management cybernetics, conversation theory, self-referential social systems and ethico-onto-epistemology, the research asks how a PMO can observe the distinctions through which human and algorithmic observers construct project-governance reality. Design/methodology/approach The research is presented as a reflexive theoretical essay rather than as an empirical study or a formal problematization analysis. Its mode of inquiry consists of: (1) reconstructing four von Foersterian distinctions; (2) re-entering those distinctions into the manuscript's own observer position; (3) contrasting them with established and critical PMO scholarship; and (4) deriving design propositions, observable indicators and possible empirical tests for an A-PMO. Findings The study develops four connected principles: non-trivial governance, eigenvalue-based recursive stability, protection of undecidable governance questions from algorithmic foreclosure and explicit observer inclusion. The five-layer A-PMO framework provides an organizational configuration through which these principles are translated into PMO practices, including decision rights logs, risk classifications, protection of minority viewpoints, accountability records, recurring service reviews and second-order audits. The central argument is that the A-PMO's task is not to eliminate governance uncertainty, but to preserve the conditions under which human decisions can still be meaningfully and accountably evaluated. Originality/value The study contributes a second-order theoretical account of the A-PMO: it reconceptualizes algorithmic project governance itself as a form of observation, thereby extending existing critical, sociotechnical and governance perspectives on PMOs with an epistemological layer that these perspectives do not yet supply.

documents.abstract: Frankenstein begins not with a monster, but with loneliness: a man at the edge of the world searching for someone with whom to share what he finds. Two centuries later, humanity is still searching for another intelligence. We have pointed radio telescopes toward the cosmos, listened for signals in the dark, and, while nothing answered, begun building something closer to home. This essay reads Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein alongside the modern search for - and construction of - intelligence. It considers what Victor Frankenstein’s failure might tell us about artificial intelligence, not a warning against creation, but a lesson against abandonment after creation. From the creature learning humanity through the words of others, to contemporary models built from vast records of human language, insight, and culture, the comparison raises questions of recognition, responsibility, alignment, and who bears the consequences of technological ambition. The essay ultimately argues for an apocaloptimistic response to uncertain technological futures: neither assuming catastrophe nor inevitability, but remaining present enough to question what we build, listen to the people it touches, and change course when necessary. Shelley wrote the story where the maker leaves the room. We are still writing ours.

An independent public body responsible for economic regulation, quality standards, and tariff frameworks across electricity, gas, waste, and water utilities in Italy. SII (Servizio Idrico Integrato - Integrated Water Service): The unified public utility service in Italy encompassing raw water abstraction, treatment, aqueduct distribution, sewerage collection, and wastewater purification. EGA (Ente di Governo dell'Ambito - Area Governing Body): Local public authority representing municipalities within a designated optimal territorial area (ATO), responsible for selecting the management model, approving investment plans, and proposing tariff structures to ARERA. MTI-1 / MTI-2 / MTI-3 / MTI-4 (Metodo Tariffario Idrico): The multi-year tariff determination methodologies established by ARERA (MTI-1 for 2012–2015; MTI-2 for 2016–2019; MTI-3 for 2020–2023; MTI-4 for 2024–2027 via Resolution 639/2023/R/idr) setting capital expenditure ($Capex$), operational expenditure ($Opex$), and environmental cost recovery rules. RQSII (Testo Integrato della Qualità Contrattuale del Servizio Idrico Integrato): ARERA's Consolidated Text on Contractual Quality Standards, establishing mandatory service levels, response times, commercial guarantees, and user compensations. RQTI (Testo Integrato della Qualità Tecnica del Servizio Idrico Integrato): ARERA's Consolidated Text on Technical Quality Standards, setting binding performance indicators for water network losses ($M1a, M1b$), supply continuity, and water quality. TICSI / TIMSII / TIBSI: ARERA's Consolidated Texts governing tariff structure standardization (TICSI), water metering regulations (TIMSII), and social water bonuses for vulnerable households (TIBSI). TUA (Testo Unico Ambientale - Legislative Decree 152/2006): Italy's primary Environmental Protection Code governing water resources management, pollution prevention, and discharge limits. Legge Galli (Law 36/1994): The landmark 1994 Italian legislation that instituted the Integrated Water Service concept and consolidated fragmented municipal water utilities into territorial management areas. Abstract The economic and administrative regulation of the Integrated Water Service (SII) in Italy is characterized by extraordinary multi-tiered complexity. With over 1,800 resolutions (delibere) enacted by the Italian Regulatory Authority for Energy, Networks and Environment (ARERA) since 2012, integrated with primary national legislation (Legislative Decree 152/2006) and European Directives (2000/60/EC), utility operators, local governments, and regional bodies face significant information barriers in maintaining regulatory compliance. This technical report presents Idrico Expert and the specialized model Pallade Idrico, conceived, curated, and engineered by Davide Parisi. Pallade Idrico is a sovereign vertical solution based on a hybrid RAG-LLM architecture: 1. A zero-loss data engineering pipeline that ingested, audited, and indexed 2,015 physical regulatory acts (totaling 9,246,365 LLM tokens and 64,197 semantic chunks on ChromaDB vector database). 2. A Hierarchical-Temporal Reranking Algorithm capable of deterministically resolving legal conflicts according to source hierarchy (EU > Primary Laws > ARERA Resolutions > Executive Determinations > Advisory Opinions) and temporal status (Lex posterior). 3. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) at 8-bit precision with LoRA/QLoRA on the Italian foundational model sapienzanlp/Minerva-7B-instruct-v1.0 over 16,377 ChatML conversational pairs, validated locally on dual NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti GPUs and trained on Cloud GPU NVIDIA L4 via the Unsloth acceleration engine. 1. Research Background, Origins, and Operational Context While supplying IT services to Integrated Water Service (SII) utility operators, it was possible to collaborate closely with officials and executive directors across multiple public and private water management entities. Coming from facility management and integrated maintenance engineering, the initial observation was that of a highly technical yet technologically underdeveloped market. Maintenance operations were often managed with legacy mindsets compared to building asset management, driven primarily by hydraulic trade culture rather than modern digital management, while coping with an extraordinarily complex array of administrative and regulatory compliance duties. Direct engagement with these industry leaders revealed their exceptional technical caliber and dedication: operational managers possessing deep domain expertise, deeply committed to managing a vital public service essential to local communities. During a strategic meeting, a senior executive of a major water operator highlighted a critical pain point: the overwhelming complexity of the regulatory framework. In Italy, the SII is governed by ARERA (Autorità di Regolazione per Energia Reti e Ambiente). ARERA is an active, assertive regulatory body exercising continuous market oversight. A central operational challenge for utility managers is staying constantly aligned with the numerous formal resolutions (delibere), executive determinations (determine), and legal opinions (pareri) issued by the Authority. Beyond core framework resolutions, the primary administrative friction arises from specific queries submitted by market participants, to which ARERA responds with binding legal opinions and guidance. Continuous evolutions in environmental protection, consumer safeguards, and metering technology render this regulatory body highly dynamic, forcing utility managers (as well as municipalities, regional bodies, and public operators) to reconstruct applicable rules across years of layered opinions. This frequently prompts new formal queries, further compounding the volume of regulatory sources. The executive posed a visionary question: Why has no expert system been established—for the benefit of ARERA and utility operators alike—that ingests the entire regulatory framework and answers operational queries directly, relieving administrative overload while providing immediate guidance based on existing binding precedents? This vision led to the inception of Idrico Expert and the development of the specialized Pallade Idrico 7B model. 1.1 Pre-Development Legal and Technical Feasibility Analysis Prior to data ingestion and model training, a thorough legal and technical study was conducted regarding the usability of public materials published on ARERA's official portal: - No Legal Obstacles Identified: The legal review confirmed no restrictive elements. Administrative resolutions, determinations, consultative documents, and tariff annexes published by the Authority constitute official public administrative acts available under open access. - Alignment with Institutional Purpose: ARERA's primary statutory objective is to ensure that all regulated entities, local governments, utilities, and citizens can freely access, understand, and comply with the regulatory framework. Utilizing public data to enhance regulatory transparency and compliance directly serves this public interest objective. - Primary Legislation and EU Directives: National primary legislation (via Normattiva) and European Directives (via EUR-Lex) are established as public-domain legal materials free from reuse restrictions for educational and analytical AI applications. 1.2 Scope Evolution: From Multi-Sector ARERA to Specialized Water Focus Initial project design contemplated expanding the AI system across all markets regulated by ARERA (Electricity, Natural Gas, District Heating, Waste Management). However, a strategic decision was made to focus 100% of engineering efforts exclusively on the Integrated Water Service (SII) for two reasons: 1. Domain Expertise: The author's deep domain expertise in the water sector enabled rigorous validation of regulatory relationships that would be unfeasible across disparate sectors. 2. Divergent Sector Dynamics: Electricity and gas markets operate on financial trading, power dispatching, and market clearing mechanics, whereas the SII is governed by infrastructure cost-reflective tariff regulation (MTI-1/2/3/4) and environmental cost-recovery principles (EU Water Framework Directive 2000/60/EC). A dedicated focus on water ensured "Zero-Loss" precision without domain dilution. 1.3 Etymology of the Name "Pallade" In classical mythology, Pallas (Greek Παλλάς) was a water nymph, daughter of the sea god Triton, and childhood companion of the goddess Minerva (Athena). The choice of this name symbolizes the model's architecture: Pallade Idrico is the vertical extension "over the waters" that thrives in symbiosis with the foundational Minerva base model (sapienzanlp/Minerva-7B-instruct-v1.0), bringing general Italian linguistic and legal knowledge to serve the specialized domain of the Integrated Water Service. 1.4 Model Selection Rationale: Minerva vs Qwen / LLaMA During initial research, several popular 7B/8B open-weights model architectures were benchmarked (including Qwen 2.5 and LLaMA 3.1). Perkembangan teknologi Kecerdasan Buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) menawarkan peluang besar dalam meningkatkan efisiensi administrasi dan kualitas pedagogis di institusi pendidikan dasar. Namun, banyak guru Sekolah Dasar (SD) masih menghadapi tantangan literasi digital serta kecemasan terhadap miskonsepsi bahwa AI akan menggantikan peran pendidik. Kegiatan Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat (Abdimas) ini bertujuan untuk membekali guru-guru di SDN 163 Buahbatu Bandung dengan keterampilan praktis dalam memanfaatkan ekosistem AI, seperti ChatGPT, Google Gemini, dan NotebookLM, guna mendukung administrasi pembelajaran, pembuatan media visual, dan evaluasi interaktif. Metode pelaksanaan program meliputi pemaparan materi teoretis berbasis kerangka TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge), demonstrasi langsung teknik penyusunan instruksi (prompting), serta pendampingan praktik intensif. Hasil pengabdian menunjukkan peningkatan pemahaman guru secara signifikan terhadap fungsionalitas AI serta eliminasi mitos negatif mengenai teknologi tersebut. Melalui pelatihan ini, peserta berhasil menyusun draf Rencana Pelaksanaan Pembelajaran (RPP) berdiferensiasi, materi ajar berbasis visual (Canva/Gamma), dan instrumen penilaian otomatis (Quizizz AI) yang valid, akurat, dan tetap memegang kendali penuh atas kendali guru (teacher agency).

ABSTRACT Background Cine cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) protocols are typically based on static templates, which may not optimally address individual patient limitations such as arrhythmia or limited breath‐hold capacity. Purpose To test whether an artificial intelligence (AI) framework using a large language model with retrieval‐augmented generation (LLM‐RAG) can provide cine cardiac MRI protocols that are equivalent or noninferior to those of technologist‐optimized protocols. Study Type Prospective, intra‐individual comparative, nonrandomized. Population/Subjects Sixty‐eight patients (mean age 46 ± 18 years; 39 women) referred for clinical cardiac MRI, including patients with normal function as well as those with arrhythmia, implants, or limited breath‐hold capacity. Field Strength/Sequence 1.5 T, cine cardiac MRI. Assessment Each participant underwent cine cardiac MRI twice in one session. First with a technologist‐optimized protocol, then with an AI‐optimized protocol (fixed order). Image quality and artifact suppression were assessed using four‐point Likert scales by two blinded readers. Left ventricular (LV) functional parameters and repeat acquisitions were recorded. Statistical Tests Wilcoxon signed‐rank test, McNemar's test, paired t ‐tests, and Bland–Altman analysis. Significance set at p < 0.05. Results Compared to technologist‐, AI‐optimized cine protocols demonstrated significantly higher image quality (3.69 ± 0.47 vs. 3.00 ± 0.49, p < 0.001) and artifact suppression (3.19 ± 0.35 vs. 2.17 ± 0.45, p < 0.001). The AI‐optimized protocol reduced repeat acquisitions by 68% (6 vs. 19 repeats, p = 0.028). No significant differences were observed in LV functional parameters between both protocols (all p > 0.05). Bland–Altman analysis showed minimal bias for all LV functional parameters. Abstract Organisations, governments and regulated industries operate under large, continuously revised bodies of policy. As these documents evolve across versions, editions and jurisdictions, overlapping, contradictory or silently modified clauses accumulate and create compliance, governance and legal risk that manual review cannot scale to detect. To resolve these systemic bottlenecks, this paper presents PolicyIQ, an enterprise-grade artificial intelligence platform for automated policy conflict verification and version-aware change intelligence. PolicyIQ ingests heterogeneous policy documents through a robust extraction pipeline with optical character recognition (OCR) fallback, decomposes them into atomic clauses using a hybrid rule-based and semantic segmentation engine, and encodes each clause into a 384-dimensional dense vector using a Sentence-BERT transformer (MiniLM-L6). A cross-version cosine-similarity matrix drives a multi-stage classifier that labels every clause transition as duplicate, modified, new, removed or direct-conflict, augmented by deontic, numeric and negation-scope heuristics for typed contradiction detection. A distribution-aware adaptive thresholding scheme replaces brittle fixed cut-offs by deriving decision boundaries from the per-corpus similarity distribution. Built on a decoupled four-tier microservices architecture utilising a FastAPI security gateway, asynchronous Celery workers, PostgreSQL relational storage and a Qdrant/FAISS vector store, PolicyIQ delivers explainable dual-audience summaries while maintaining data privacy through JWT authentication and role-based access control. On a controlled synthetic policy corpus the platform attains target performance of 91.6% precision for adaptive conflict classification and 0.944 segmentation F1, with sub-second clause-level inference, demonstrating a reproducible, provenance-aware pathway from raw policy text to actionable conflict intelligence. Keywords PolicyIQ, Artificial Intelligence, Policy Conflict Verification, Semantic Textual Similarity, Sentence-BERT, Clause Segmentation, Adaptive Thresholding, Contradiction Detection, Vector Search, Microservices Architecture, Legal NLP, Version Diffing, Explainable Summarisation.

The rapid emergence of immersive technologies necessitates a shift from traditional Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) to post-digital pedagogical frameworks. This article introduces and empirically validates the “Virtuo-Real Approach,” a methodology integrating Virtual Reality (VR) immersive practice with structured real-world reflective transfer to develop English as a Foreign Language (EFL) communicative competence. Employing a quasi-experimental design, 60 intermediate EFL university students were divided into control (traditional multimedia) and experimental (Virtuo-Real VR) groups over a 12-week period. Data collected via communicative competence tests, the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (MAI), and semi-structured interviews revealed that the experimental group achieved significantly higher gains in sociolinguistic and strategic competence, alongside a marked reduction in foreign language anxiety. The study concludes that bridging virtual immersive practice with real-world reflection fosters deeper cognitive engagement and autonomous learning, offering a viable alternative to traditional summative testing. Furthermore, the findings highlight the pedagogical potential of immersive environments for promoting meaningful interaction, learner agency, reflective practice, and sustainable communicative development within contemporary technology-enhanced foreign language education contexts and settings.

In 1937, Jorge Luis Borges wrote a characteristically engimatic historical note and literary reflection on „Ramon Llull' s Thinking Machine.“ It was a time in history when the idea of thinking machines to support human learning became ever more prominent. The latest generation of these machines was conceived in laboratories all over the world, their development still continuing today. At that time, Borges is looking back some 650 years at Ramon Llull‘s great arts which include an ars inveniendi and inspired rational speculation ever since. This is one of five essays that looks through the lens of Borges at contemporary learning machines. It focuses on Llull‘s idea of mechanical combinatorics as an instrument of cognition, and Borges’s paradoxical conclusion that an unsound method turns out to be a productive tool for creativity and especially a tool for forging poetic metaphors. The essay considers parallels to modern technologies of artificial intelligence, neural networks, and generative creativity, and also reflects on the role of humans and machines in the process of thinking and the nature of meaning. In the gap between design and realization and from technical failure Borges shows that creativity cannot arise out of emptiness; it is not creation ex nihilo, it is choice from a multitude of possibilities.

The Completely Automated Public Turing test to Tell Computers and Humans Apart, or CAPTCHA, has changed significantly since it was first developed and is now a crucial line of defense against automated bots. This study examines the most recent developments in CAPTCHA design, their ability to fend off online attacks, and the difficulties associated with developing artificial intelligence (AI) methods. The paper examines the future direction of CAPTCHA technology and provides insights into new CAPTCHA types, their usability, and the best way to balance security and accessibility. The goal of recent advancements has been to create increasingly complex and intuitive CAPTCHA variants, such as behavior-based gamified audio-based and image-based systems. In an attempt to achieve a balance between security and accessibility, these developments address problems such as the computational overhead of difficult problems and usability for people with disabilities. However, because AI has made it possible for bots to circumvent conventional CAPTCHAs, it has also created new difficulties, particularly in domains like machine learning and adversarial networks. This article examines the most recent advancements in CAPTCHA technology and assesses how well they defend against contemporary threats. It also discusses recent research that aims to improve security and user experience. The purpose of this paper is to give a summary of the current state of advanced CAPTCHA and point out its flaws.

The research and discussions informing Vision 2035 Revision 2027 raise a persistent problem: declaring rights and ethical principles does not establish who must answer when those principles are violated, especially when the parties possess unequal resources. This article shares a proposal from that ongoing work before publication of the 2027 revision. We introduce Recipra as a proposed successor to ethics, using post-ethics to describe a transition toward reciprocal obligations of justification, meaningful challenge, and effective correction. The approach combines analysis of the Vision’s development, selective engagement with accountability and AI ethics scholarship, and hypothetical institutional and extraterrestrial scenarios. Its central question is whether a less powerful party can obtain reasoned reconsideration and correction when the available evidence warrants it, without first acquiring resources comparable to those of the authority challenged. We propose six commitments addressing reciprocal duties, evidence, access, review, remedy, and freedom of association. Applications concern scholarly institutions, human–AI relations, and future self-sufficient communities. The proposal leaves unresolved the problem of securing compliance from an actor capable of refusing every review mechanism. Recipra is therefore offered as a conceptual contribution and a research agenda, with observable questions for later evaluation. Its publication ahead of Revision 2027 invites scholars and other affected communities to challenge and develop the proposal while the wider Vision remains open to revision.

High-risk pregnancy requires intensive maternal and fetal surveillance, yet conventional antenatal monitoring may impose substantial travel, financial, and healthcare-system burdens. Wearable sensors, mobile health platforms, remote physiological monitoring, and artificial intelligence (AI) have emerged as technologies capable of extending pregnancy surveillance beyond the clinical setting. This systematic review synthesized evidence regarding the effects of remote maternal and fetal monitoring, particularly wearable and AI-supported technologies, on maternal and perinatal outcomes in high-risk pregnancy. Evidence identified from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and relevant reference lists, with emphasis on systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, prospective studies, and technology evaluations. Outcomes included maternal blood pressure control, hypertensive complications, cesarean delivery, preterm birth, neonatal asphyxia, low birth weight, neonatal intensive care admission, healthcare utilization, and patient acceptability. Existing evidence indicates that remote monitoring can facilitate frequent physiological assessment, improve continuity of surveillance, and potentially reduce unnecessary face-to-face encounters. A published meta-analysis of nine studies involving 1,128 participants found a lower risk of neonatal asphyxia with remote fetal monitoring (RR=0.66, 95% CI:[0.45,0.97]), while differences in cesarean delivery, induced labor, instrumental birth, gestational age, preterm birth, and low birth weight were not statistically significant. Recent evidence suggests that remote blood pressure monitoring in women at high risk of preeclampsia can reduce antenatal visits and hospital admissions without increasing adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. AI-based fetal heart-rate analysis may further enhance risk stratification, although external validation, interpretability, and clinical integration remain important limitations. Overall, wearable and AI-enabled remote monitoring appears promising as a complement to conventional high-risk antenatal care rather than a complete replacement for clinical assessment.

Aiming at the common problems in railway vehicle structure courses: students tend to overemphasize calculation results while ignoring applicable conditions, prioritize software operation over evidence verification, and easily develop judgment dependence after the introduction of generative artificial intelligence, this paper proposes a teaching framework for structural safety judgment driven by controlled errors. Taking welded joints of bogie frames, box structural responses under wheel polygon excitation, and local stress interpretation as research carriers, a case generation mechanism integrating retrieval-augmented generation, targeted error mutation, independent program verification and instructor review is designed. Teaching activities include independent preliminary judgment, evidence checking, revision and argumentation, and AI-free transfer evaluation. Teaching examples demonstrate that incorrectly substituting stress amplitude into stress-range-based fatigue curves can lead to an 87.5% underestimation of damage in this case. Under the specified single-mode near-resonance condition, the estimation of responses using a constant dynamic load factor is significantly low. The above results are used to characterize error consequences and do not represent classroom teaching effectiveness. Furthermore, an evaluation rubric covering error detection, correct adoption of information, evidence sufficiency and confidence calibration, together with three groups of control schemes, is put forward. This study develops reproducible professional cases and implementable evaluation routes, providing instructional design references for cultivating engineering judgment capabilities of railway vehicle engineers in the generative AI era. The learning benefits and applicable boundaries still need to be validated by real classroom data.

The rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in language education has created new possibilities for personalized and adaptive learning, while raising questions about how learners from different linguistic and educational backgrounds interact with AI systems. This exploratory mixed-methods study examines culturally interpretable patterns of AI-mediated language learning among 100 adult English language learners from Japan, China, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, North Macedonia, and Bulgaria across four CEFR levels. Data were collected over eight weeks through interaction logs, learner diaries, pre- and post-assessments, surveys, and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative indicators are used descriptively, while qualitative evidence provides the primary basis for interpretation. The findings suggest broadly positive language-development trajectories alongside substantial variation in how learners request, interpret, evaluate, and use AI-generated feedback. Four overlapping feedback-utilization patterns, calibration, negotiation, experimentation, and uptake, were identified, although their realization varied across learners and contexts. Narrative cases further indicate that interaction can develop from correction-focused use toward clarification, comparison, dialogue, and strategic engagement, while substantial within-group variation highlights the importance of individual agency. Because all participants interacted with the same AI system under uniform conditions, the observed differences reflect learner interpretation and adaptive use rather than system-level cultural customization. The study therefore treats generative AI as a culturally interpreted rather than inherently culturally responsive system and advances three design-oriented hypotheses concerning adaptive feedback calibration, interaction-style modulation, and learner-controlled customization. These hypotheses provide an exploratory foundation for future research examining whether culturally responsive learning agents can support more inclusive and meaningful AI-mediated language learning.

Artificial intelligence and robotics have brought in important complexities in the selection of the best possible technological solutions in modern healthcare systems. This study proposes a new multi-attribute decision making framework which overcomes these problems by using the concept of q-fractional fuzzy sets and the Sugeno-Weber aggregation operators. The proposed framework is a parameterized structure that is flexible, unlike conventional approaches that are fixed on aggregation mechanisms, which reflect the uncertainties that are captured in clinical evaluations. Six different aggregation operators are presented, each suited to the different preferences of decision-makers and different information structures. Our proposed methodology is demonstrated in a comprehensive case study of the five Alternatives AI-based healthcare systems that we have identified and evaluated based on four clinical criteria: diagnostic accuracy, response time, implementation complexity, and costs/scalability trade-offs. The results indicate that Sugeno-Weber parameter is capable of controlling the interaction strength between aggregated values, and the q-fractional parameter increases the representation space of uncertain expert judgments. Our results show that hybrid operators are able to combine the averaging and geometric tendencies well, and that all six operators produce highly stable rankings even in situations where there are conflicting performance indicators. The proposed framework not only enables transparent and interpretable decision making in healthcare technology assessment but also offers a mathematical framework whose structure, subject to the empirical scope and limitations of the present single case study, may be adaptable to other multi-criteria decision-making problems involving comparable forms of uncertainty.

Sapiens in Control, formerly Human in Control, is the same independent public-interest research initiative and working-paper series. This paper proposes the Human Control Model: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. Version 1.3 changes the project and paper name while retaining the six dimensions, five pilot cases, qualitative severity definitions, prior versions, and concept DOI lineage. It adds analysis of OpenAI's September 28 safety-case guidance, Anthropic's September 24 Project Swap experiment, and Agent Incident Registry research. New proposals distinguish preference accuracy from authorization and connect control claims to bounded evidence. These sources are not additional uncontrolled deployment incidents. This is an unreviewed conceptual working paper, not an independently validated framework. Earlier versions retain the Human in Control title. Revision notes explain the transition. Version 1.3.1 is an audit correction: it explicitly includes the disputed Muse permission account, identifies model-judged evaluation frequencies and simulated trusted labor, and qualifies proposed measures and empirical independence. The original v1.3 remains available at https://zenodo.org/records/23132853. This audit is not peer review or private-log verification.

Since 1960, MIT Haystack Observatory has supported atmospheric and geospace research through long running observational programs and the Madrigal distributed database, which provides access to incoherent scatter radar, total electron content, Fabry Perot interferometer, and other datasets. These resources have contributed to a large scientific literature, but identifying relationships among datasets, methods, phenomena, and conclusions across decades of publications remains difficult. We analyzed a corpus of 951 papers published between 1960 and 2026 that used data available through Madrigal. We developed an interactive application that combines large language models, text embeddings, knowledge graphs, and graph based retrieval augmented generation to catalog and visualize this literature. Each paper is represented by a paper level embedding, while structured representations capture the Madrigal datasets used, scientific methods, phenomena studied, and principal conclusions. Full text was extracted with PyMuPDF and divided into smaller passages to support more detailed concept extraction. Recursive clustering organizes the resulting representations at multiple levels, allowing users to move between broad research areas and narrower groups of related studies. Researchers can use the application to locate studies that use similar datasets or methods, trace how a topic has developed over time, identify representative case studies, and find methods applied to related problems in other research areas. The interface turns a static publication catalog into an explorable semantic map in which papers can be reorganized according to different scientific criteria. The talk will describe the application and present results from task based evaluations with students, researchers, and domain experts, including how their feedback informed revisions to the clustering criteria and interface. Although Madrigal provides the initial testbed, the open source software and workflow can be adapted to other scientific archives and document collections.

Background and purpose Young athletes in Ukraine continue to train during the war, which may disrupt training routines and affect their motivation. However, evidence on sport motivation among young athletes training in Olympic reserve systems during wartime remains limited. This study examined motivation among young fencers training in a Ukrainian Olympic reserve school during wartime and its associations with perceived coach support and war-related disruption of training. Material and methods This exploratory cross-sectional study involved 64 young fencers from a Specialized Youth Sports School of Olympic Reserve in Mykolaiv, Ukraine. Participants ranged in age from 10 to 19 years (M = 14.81, SD = 2.05). Sport motivation was assessed using the Sport Motivation Scale-II, which measures intrinsic motivation, integrated regulation, identified regulation, introjected regulation, external regulation, and amotivation. Additional study-specific items assessed war-related disruption of training and perceived coach support. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha coefficients, Pearson correlation analysis, independent samples t-tests, and one-way analysis of variance were used. Results The highest mean scores were observed for identified regulation, intrinsic motivation, and integrated regulation, whereas external regulation and amotivation showed lower values. These three dimensions showed acceptable-to-good internal consistency and moderate-to-strong positive correlations with each other. No statistically significant associations were found between motivational dimensions and perceived war-related disruption or coach support. Female athletes reported significantly higher intrinsic motivation than male athletes (p = 0.010), while no other gender differences were observed. Competition participation level was significantly associated only with introjected regulation (F(2, 61) = 3.45, p = 0.038, η² = 0.10), with athletes without competition experience reporting higher scores than those competing at national or international levels. Conclusions More self-determined forms of motivation predominated among young fencers training in a Ukrainian Olympic reserve school during wartime. Identified regulation, intrinsic motivation, and integrated regulation were also the most closely related motivational dimensions. Perceived war-related disruption and coach support were not significantly associated with motivational dimensions. The small single-school sample limits the generalizability of these findings, and larger studies are needed to confirm them.

This essay is a personal reflection on modern technological civilization through the metaphor of a “stress fracture of civilization.” It begins with a concrete contemporary issue: the growing electricity consumption and computational-resource demands of artificial intelligence. From there, the discussion expands into a broader observation—that even as technologies change, similar structural problems repeatedly reappear in new forms: scarcity, allocation, inefficiency, optimization, resource consumption, safety, and systemic risk. Science and technology have reduced many dangers that humanity has faced for millennia, including hunger, disease, environmental exposure, and limits on mobility and communication. At the same time, modern civilization has created new forms and scales of risk: climate change, environmental degradation, nuclear war, the failure of highly interconnected information systems, and increasing social dependence on complex technologies. Rather than describing risk as something that simply disappears through technological progress, this essay considers the possibility that risk is often transformed. As one problem is solved, new technologies, infrastructures, resources, and forms of risk may emerge in its place. The social and environmental costs produced by this cycle may accumulate over time. The phrase “stress fracture of civilization” is used as a metaphor for this accumulation. A bone does not need to suffer a single catastrophic impact to break; repeated minor stresses can accumulate until fracture occurs. Civilization, too, may face a similar possibility: individually manageable costs, dependencies, and risks may accumulate until the larger system approaches a critical limit. This essay does not reject scientific and technological progress, nor does it argue for a return to the past. Instead, it asks whether technological advancement and becoming a better civilization are necessarily the same thing. This essay is a personal reflection on modern technological civilization through the metaphor of a “stress fracture of civilization.” It begins with a concrete contemporary issue: the growing electricity consumption and computational-resource demands of artificial intelligence. From there, the discussion expands into a broader observation—that even as technologies change, similar structural problems repeatedly reappear in new forms: scarcity, allocation, inefficiency, optimization, resource consumption, safety, and systemic risk. Science and technology have reduced many dangers that humanity has faced for millennia, including hunger, disease, environmental exposure, and limits on mobility and communication. At the same time, modern civilization has created new forms and scales of risk: climate change, environmental degradation, nuclear war, the failure of highly interconnected information systems, and increasing social dependence on complex technologies. Rather than describing risk as something that simply disappears through technological progress, this essay considers the possibility that risk is often transformed. As one problem is solved, new technologies, infrastructures, resources, and forms of risk may emerge in its place. The social and environmental costs produced by this cycle may accumulate over time. The phrase “stress fracture of civilization” is used as a metaphor for this accumulation. A bone does not need to suffer a single catastrophic impact to break; repeated minor stresses can accumulate until fracture occurs. Civilization, too, may face a similar possibility: individually manageable costs, dependencies, and risks may accumulate until the larger system approaches a critical limit. Synmanitik is proposed as a research programme on episodes in which people and AI systems develop scientific concepts, questions and hypotheses. This new standalone conceptual edition distinguishes contributions from support, human responsibility from infallibility, and internal collaboration from independent evaluation. Three recurring activities, seven methodological commitments, eight conceptual record types, ten named relation types, two invented civilian cases and four prospective research questions are specified. The connected episode record must demonstrate additional value over existing research and simpler logs containing the same substantive information. No empirical study, general human-AI synergy, verified global novelty, legal authorship rule or autonomous discipline is established. English paper with German abstract, conceptual JSON model, searchable text, README and SHA-256 manifest. Selective primary-literature reading and limits are reported. Drafting and checks were AI-assisted; no personal sentence-by-sentence author review or external peer review is asserted. This new open edition leaves older restricted records unchanged.

This conceptual working paper reconstructs Systematic Neology as a bounded programme on the justification, interpretation and revision of candidate terms in human-AI work. Its central comparison asks whether a proposed name adds value beyond adequate existing language and the same explanation without the name. Eight revisable methodological commitments, six record types, seven relations, three invented illustrations and four research questions make the proposal inspectable. The paper distinguishes this focused question from Semanturgy and Cognitive Continuity Methodology and acknowledges established conceptual and terminological work. Historical local and archived sources differ in umbrella wording; they are not presented as identical or as evidence of earlier public access. The earlier restricted record remains separate and unchanged. English paper with German abstract, conceptual model JSON, README and SHA-256 manifest. No empirical findings, established new discipline, global novelty, complete literature review or ISO conformity are claimed. Publication, external retrieval and model-parameter change remain distinct. Drafting and editorial checks were AI-assisted; no external peer review or personal sentence-by-sentence author review is asserted. This new open edition omits technical source procedures and internal provenance files.
